subtopic: MANNING AND OPERATION OF DISTANT EARLY WARNING LINE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MANNING AND OPERATION OF DISTANT EARLY WARNING LINE
speechtext:
On March 20, Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence made a statement respecting the manning and operation of the distant early warning line and a number of questions were asked afterwards which I should like to deal with at this time. I wish to emphasize at the outset that this distant early warning line and other radar stations which have been discussed from time to time are for continental and not exclusively Canadian defence, just as certain joint defence projects in western Europe are for collective rather than merely national defence. That being the case, it seems to be appropriate that the United States, as the larger country with the most
Inquiries of the Ministry at stake, should have a major share of responsibility for these joint defence projects, even though they may be situated in Canadian territory.
As hon. members will recall, on February 22, 1955, I explained Canada's role in providing our share of these continental early warning arrangements. I pointed out then that as part of the over-all effort Canada had undertaken to finance, construct and operate the mid-Canada line. I also indicated that following joint Canada-United States announcements, which were made some months previously, and copies of which I tabled at that time, the United States had undertaken responsibility for the construction of a distant early warning line. Subsequently, an agreement, in the form of an exchange of notes, was made with the United States covering the construction of this line in Canadian territory. That agreement was tabled by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on May 20 last. It outlines in detail the conditions under which the United States was authorized to build the line in the interest of the defence of our two countries. It also preserves, as the minister said, the principle enunciated in the joint declaration of February 12, 1947, on defence co-operation that all co-operative arrangements will be without impairment of the control of either country over all activities in its own territory.
If hon. members will recall, it was indicated in the exchange of notes that the United States would carry out construction of the distant early warning system through a management contractor appointed by the United States, and that in fact is what happened. They will also note amongst other things that Canadian contractors would be extended equal consideration with United States contractors in the awarding of construction contracts; that, as far as practicable, electronics equipment would be manufactured in Canada; that preference would be given to Canadian labour; that nothing shall derogate from the application of Canadian law in Canada.
Experience with respect to the construction phase of that line has been very satisfactory. Contracts have been awarded to two Canadian construction firms, Foundation Company of Canada Limited and another, the Northern Construction and J. W. Stewart Limited, who are employing Canadian labour. A large number of subcontracts for goods, materials and services connected with construction have gone to Canadian firms. Very substantial contracts for air transportation have been placed with Canadian carriers, and a number of contracts for electronic material have been awarded

Inquiries of the Ministry to Canadian firms. The closest liaison between the appropriate United States and Canadian authorities has been maintained from the outset of the program, and is still being carried on to ensure that the progress of the work is facilitated and the terms and the spirit of the agreement are observed.
This agreement for the construction of the line also stated, in paragraph 7, that the extent of Canadian participation in the initial operation and manning of the D.E.W. system would be a matter for later decision by Canada after consultation with the United States. That consultation took place and a decision covering the first three years was announced-the announcement that was made on March 20 by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer).
The same general terms and conditions laid down in the agreement for the construction of the line are to apply in its manning and operation, and these, as has been pointed out, fully safeguard Canadian rights and laws.
Now, I come first to the question the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked about contractors. The answer is that, while the civilian prime contractor for the D.E.W. line, for the construction phase, was a United States firm, there was, as I have pointed out, a very large participation by Canadian firms in the execution of the contract.
With respect to the operation and manning phase, proposals were invited from Canadian and United States firms and the best bid was that of the United States firm, and we were satisfied that this firm was properly selected to manage that part of the operation. In awarding this contract to the firm it has been understood that as far as possible Canadian personnel and facilities will be used in the execution of the contract. Perhaps hon. members will remember reading that within the last few days there have been applications to our employment agencies specifying the kind of qualifications that would be required and endeavouring to get as many Canadians as possible with such qualifications to take on work in that connection.	_
There has been close co-operation between the two governments in arriving at all decisions and this co-operation is expected to continue throughout the implementation of these decisions. I think the visit of inspection that has been made over the week end by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) with the secretary of defence of the United States and his deputy is just an example of the close co-operation that is maintained in that regard.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well) asked if there were any other agreements of the same nature as the one dealing with the D.E.W. line allowing, as he put it, United States contractors appointed by the United States government to take over. The hon. member also wanted to know if these contractors and their employees were subject to Canadian laws or if there was some agreement with regard to the legal standing of those people. I have perhaps gone beyond the express terms of the question because I wanted to be sure that I was not leaving out any information that hon. members might wish to have.
In addition to the D.E.W. line agreement and the leased bases agreement which I shall deal with separately there are, apart from projects for which Canada is responsible itself, eight Canada-United States defence agreements under which contracts might be let by United States authorities; but there is a stipulation in all the agreements that Canadian contractors are to be treated on the same basis as the United States contractors. Those agreements, which in every case have been tabled in the house, are as follows:
The first is the "Pinetree" radar agreement made by an exchange of notes of August 1, 1951. These notes were tabled on February 25, 1953.
The next is the global communications agreement made by an exchange of notes of November 4 and November 8, 1952, and tabled on February 25, 1953.
The third is the Goose Bay lease made by an exchange of notes of December 5, 1952, tabled on December 16, 1952, for a certain area within the R.C.A.F. station at Goose Bay.
The next is the Haines-Fairbanks pipe line agreement made by an exchange of notes of June 30, 1953, tabled on November 19, 1953.
Another exchange of notes of May 1 and May 3, 1954, deals with the Loran station at Cape Christian, Baffin island, tabled on February 22, 1955.
Another exchange of notes of June 13, 1955, provided for an extension of radar stations from the "Pinetree" radar line, tabled on February 10, 1956.
Another exchange of notes of June 15, 1955, provided for gap filler radar stations in the "Pinetree" line, tabled on February 10, 1956.
Finally, an exchange of notes on September 22, 1955, in connection with a Pepperrell pipe line from the harbour of Saint John to the base which is just outside Saint John to avoid the inconvenience and the possible danger created by trucks carrying oil moving through the city of Saint John.
It will be appreciated that Canadian contractors have been employed on the construe-

tion of a number of these installations authorized by the above agreements.
For the sake of completeness I will mention one further installation even though it does not actually appear to come within the purview of the hon. gentleman's question. On July 9, 1954, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) announced the establishment of an oceanographic research station at Shelburne, Nova Scotia, which is now being operated jointly by the Royal Canadian Navy and the United States navy under Canadian *command.
As hon. members will note when referring to the documents which were tabled, the terms of these agreements vary somewhat, but latterly we have been trying to cast them in a more or less standard form, similar to the terms of the distant early warning line agreements. In each case, except in the case of the leased bases agreement which was originally made between the United Kingdom and the United States as a wartime necessity in 1941, Canadian law is fully applicable, and it is expressly stated that Canadian law shall apply.
With respect to the leased bases agreements, it will be recalled that on May 1, 1951,
I announced in this house that agreement had been reached through the permanent joint board on defence for the voluntary relinquishment by the United States of certain rights conferred by the leased bases agreement relating to income tax, customs and excise duties, postal privileges and, most important, the jurisdiction of the courts. A formal agreement to this effect was concluded by a subsequent exchange of notes which were tabled on May 2, 1952.
In all these arrangements for the providing of facilities on our territory Canadian sovereignty is fully recognized by the United States.

maintopic: FLYING OF "STARS AND STRIPES" AT U. S. MILITARY BASES IN CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: FLYING OF "STARS AND STRIPES" AT U. S. MILITARY BASES IN CANADA
speechtext: My question relates to the subject matter of the statement made earlier by the Prime Minister. Could the Prime Minister tell the house whether the terms of the leases to the United States of the bases on Canadian soil authorize the United States authorities to fly the Stars and Stripes above the Canadian flag on those bases?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FLYING OF "STARS AND STRIPES" AT U. S. MILITARY BASES IN CANADA
speechtext: I have never heard of the Stars and Stripes being flown over the Canadian flag. Perhaps the hon. gentleman means in the place of honour, instead of the place of honour being occupied by the Canadian flag.

maintopic: FLYING OF "STARS AND STRIPES" AT U. S. MILITARY BASES IN CANADA
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FLYING OF "STARS AND STRIPES" AT U. S. MILITARY BASES IN CANADA
speechtext:
There is nothing expressed in these leases with respect to the flying of flags. I understand that there is an administrative arrangement between the R.C.A.F. and the U.S.A.F. about the flying of flags in all the places where there may be American personnel, outside of the leased bases and that the agreement provides that the Canadian flag will have the place of honour. They will both be flown at equal height. I understand that the place of honour is the left side. I understand that it was readily agreed that, it being Canadian territory, the Canadian flag should have the place of honour.
With respect to the leased bases to which my hon. friend's question refers, what we regard as the leased bases are only the base in Newfoundland and a part of the R.C.A.F. air base at Goose Bay. Of course at Goose Bay it is the R.C.A.F. base and it is the Canadian officer in command of that base who has the place of honour for the Canadian flag. It may be that within the portion of the base that is occupied by American forces the officer in command would fly the Stars and Stripes. However, there is no arrangement as to any joint occupancy nor any conflict as to occupancy of the place of honour.
On the leased base in Newfoundland proper, which lease was made under the 1941 agreement by the government of the United Kingdom, of course there was no stipulation made with respect to the Canadian flag and there has been no stipulation made since then with respect to the Canadian flag within that base, but that being an American base for which they have a long-term lease- the lease was made by the United Kingdom

Inquiries of the Ministry government for 99 years-I would imagine that the American officer commanding that base would fly the Stars and Stripes as his flag within that base. However, I have never heard of there being any conflict there with respect to the Canadian flag and I would imagine that the Canadian flag would be flown within the base just as a matter of courtesy whenever it was being visited by Canadian officers.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
With further reference to the matter just dealt with by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent),
I should like to ask this question. Would the Prime Minister say whether or not there has been any investigation into the allegations of the Whitehorse board of trade relative to what they stated were derogatory actions on the part of United States contractors in derogation of Canadian sovereignty? If so, were any representations made to the United States government in order to assure equality of opportunity for Canadian contractors which was apparently denied them in the Eagle, Alaska, D.E.W. haul?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ALLEGED DEROGATORY ACTIONS BY UNITED STATES CONTRACTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I can answer that question as I have just returned from Point Barrow where I discussed the episode. There are certain emergency lifts required in the winter months that present tremendous difficulty. Of course there are only two ways of getting a lift into certain warning line sites in Canada during the wintertime. One is by air and the other is by tractor train. In this particular case the nature of the lift was such that a particular machine was brought in for that purpose.
It is known up there as "the monster". It was built in the United States. It has wheels which are, I think, six feet in diameter, each driven by a separate motor. It is the only one of its kind in the north country and it was used for certain lifts into the D.E.W. line. As I say, it is the only way in which to get heavy material from the railhead to these sites.
I would remind all hon. members that the D.E.W. line is a protection for Canada just as much as it is a protection for the United States. It is regarded as being of tremendous importance that the two lines-the distant early warning line and the mid-Canada line -be completed on a certain date. In order to bring that about emergencies must be taken care of. This movement amounted to 

very little in dollars and cents and it seems to me to be rather ridiculous to make a great fuss about the fact that the Canadian contractor there-and it was a Canadian contractor who was installing the equipment -made use of the only suitable equipment in the area-which happened to be United States equipment-to move in certain material for the D.E.W. line.

maintopic: ALLEGED DEROGATORY ACTIONS BY UNITED STATES CONTRACTORS
speechtext: That is not the record at all.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PAUL ROBESON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration? Will the minister inform the house of the reasons for the reported refusal to admit Mr. Paul Robeson to Canada to give a series of concerts?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: PAUL ROBESON
speechtext: Yes, sir. As I think hon. members are well aware, it is not the policy of the government to admit known communists to this country, either as immigrants or as visitors. An exception has, however, been made in the case of Mr. Robeson and of one or two other persons who were coming here as artists for purposes which appeared to be purely artistic and to have nothing to do with politics in any way. It must be within the knowledge of most hon. members that Mr. Robeson made such a visit to Canada quite recently.

subtopic: PAUL ROBESON
speechtext: In February.

subtopic: PAUL ROBESON
speechtext:
It has been necessary for the government quite recently to give consideration to what attitude would be taken to applications from prospective visitors from the Soviet union to visit this country and it has been decided, as a matter of policy, not to give visas to visitors from the Soviet union who are proposing to visit Canada under the auspices of communist or communist front organizations.
When my attention was drawn to the fact that Mr. Robeson was proposing to make a tour across Canada, I felt it was proper for me to make certain inquiries as to the auspices under which that tour was being made. Having made those inquiries, it did not seem to me to be reasonable to admit from some other country a person who is a known and, I believe, a professed communist, who was coming here to perform under what were, according to the information I have, communist auspices. That, sir, is the explanation.

subtopic: PAUL ROBESON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the explanation that has just been given by the Minister of
67509-179J
Inquiries of the Ministry Citizenship and Immigration, I wonder if he would say whether it is proposed to bar the visit of the Russian women who are coming under the auspices of the Canadian Congress of Women.

subtopic: PAUL ROBESON

subtopic: PAUL ROBESON
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question, following the question I asked just now? I understood from the newspapers-I do not know anything about it-that the organization bringing Mr. Robeson was Jerome Limited. If that is a limited company, is that a communist front? Is it a legitimate company? That is the point I am raising. I think this is a matter of civil liberties. I am not in sympathy with Mr. Robeson's political views by any stretch of the imagination.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not have the opportunity to speak in this house during the debate on

the speech from the throne, the time allowed the house under the new standing orders having prevented me from doing so. That is why I avail myself of the opportunity offered by the budget debate to give my views on certain questions that are related to it and on certain others with which I will deal only briefly so as not to take too much of the time other members could use to their advantage.
I come to the suggestions I wish to make in order to bring my contribution to a worthwhile discussion. The suggestions we make here cannot all be carried out, but they are often productive of ideas and pave the way to future legislation improvements in the enforcing of regulations. Thus the government is able to introduce measures calculated to improve existing legislation. Such is the purpose of the suggestions I am about to make.
(Text):
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) was wise and made a good move when he introduced his 1954 budget and reduced some of the taxes, especially the income tax. He then pointed out the necessity for reducing expenditures and forecast a probable increase in the value of the gross national product. This inspired the confidence of the public and the manufacturers so that the goal was obtained to such an extent that the anticipated deficit has been greatly reduced and limited to $52 million.
When participating in the budget debate last year, I indicated a way in which a reduction in expenditures might be achieved and that was through a closer examination of the estimates. Another way in which improvement may be obtained, in my estimation, would be through the proper selection of government employees. The civil service commission looks after the hiring of government employees and the degree of the applicant's knowledge is the only barometer used in deciding on appointments. I believe that great care should be taken in ascertaining the moral character of the applicant, his ability to work and his desire to adequately fulfil the tasks to be performed. These other qualities in new employees would bring about efficiency in carrying out their duties and help in reducing the expenditures of the departments. The chiefs of the various departments should be men of ability and willing to supervise fully the efficiency of the employees under their control. If the staff is left without supervision in so far as quality, ability and willingness to work are concerned, this will soon result in extra expenditures.
More and more people are considering government jobs and therefore the choice should be properly made on the basis of a
The Budget-Mr. E. heduc proper investigation. With proper choice and proper supervision by the heads of the departments, the results will be advantageous and will bring about substantial savings thus leading to lower taxation. If the right kind of employees are selected, the work of the heads of the departments will be made easier. The delay before permanent appointments is made should be extended from six months to one year in order that the approval may be based on a more adequate period of review.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express an opinion as to how expenditures might be cut down. I believe that a reduction of expenditures, through a further lowering of income tax, would have stimulated business and industry and this would have been a factor of progress, as was the case last year. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) told us why he could not lower taxes this year; he said that owing to the present buoyancy of our economy, it might have brought on inflation which would have easily cancelled out the benefits of any tax reduction,
For the past few years, and especially last spring, the opposition severely criticized the Minister of Finance when he decreased taxes in the face of a probable deficit. But what has happened? Later developments proved that he was right. The opposition strongly criticized the government for real or seasonal unemployment last year and they could not believe that the situation would improve. But what happened later on? The last quarter of 1955 saw an unprecedented level of production and employment in Canada.
The opposition does not admit that the government promoted business recovery by creating a favourable atmosphere to private enterprise, but when there is a drop in production or employment, the government gets all the blame.
Again, the government is blamed when strikes slow down our economy.
But according to the opposition, when business is looking up, as it did after the war, and in 1955, they contend that the government had nothing to do with it.
Let us have criticism, but let it be constructive and not given for the mere satisfaction of criticizing. However, the public is a good judge; they have proved it many times in the past and, I am sure, they will keep on trusting the present Liberal government.
While speaking in English, a moment ago, I suggested two methods that would permit
2824	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. E. Leduc tax cuts. Here I mention them briefly in French: a close study of appropriations compared to previous appropriations; adequate hiring of government employees by the civil service commission which, besides looking into educational qualifications, should require moral training, application at work and efficiency, without forgetting that most important factor: recommendation by department heads who supervised the new employees during their trial period.
While regulations provide statutory increases in salary over a certain number of years, these should not be granted unless the supervisor is satisfied with the employee, and I submit that if such a provision were included in the application forms, the chief of a division would make sure of the efficiency of the employee before granting his final approval.
The civil service commission should provide in addition to the basic salary, yearly increase which would go only to deserving, faithful and punctual employees.
In my opinion, the pre-permanency trial period should cover twelve months instead of six months in order to give department heads proper time to assess a new employee's skills and the value of his work. Thus, the increase would go only to the deserving.
Let us now mention a matter which concerns the Department of National Revenue. I refer to the rate of interest claimed on anticipated tax payments by merchants, salesmen on commission, etc., in cases of insufficient payments. This rate does not sound fair to me, since payments are based on a future income assessment.
If the taxpayer has obtained an income higher than the amount foreseen in his estimate, he is penalized by a 6 per cent interest, while if he has overestimated his probable income and made his payments accordingly, he receives but a 3 per cent interest for the overpayment.
I do not believe that a penalty should be levied unless the taxpayer has underestimated his income by more than 10 per cent. A taxpayer sometimes finds it difficult to determine in advance his exact net income. Since the departmental officer has no leeway and must apply the law as it stands, a margin of 10 per cent should be tolerated.
The taxpayer who is of good faith does not relish the fact that he has to pay interest. If my suggestion were accepted, it would avoid much resentment on the part of taxpayers, especially since between the final date for the payment of the tax, that is April 30, 

and the date when his return is assessed there is a few months' delay. If an error is found, the taxpayer must pay for the delay between the time when his return was filed and the time when it was checked.
I draw the matter to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue in the hope that he may remedy this deficiency and apply the law in a more equitable way.
I believe that the provincial income tax act contains a provision to that effect and it seems to be the only provision of that act which is sound. However, I make it a point to mention it.
The federal government has created a favourable atmosphere for the expansion of business and industry.
Today the eyes of the world are turned towards Canada. An energetic and determined nation as ours, with its oil, its iron ore and uranium, with its forests and its mines, with its farms and its manufactures, can show right here what it can accomplish given the necessary will, leadership and resources.
The records achieved by our domestic and international trade, by our agricultural and industrial revenues, by the new constructions and investments prove the wisdom of our population and the vision of its leaders.
The main cause of Canadian prosperity is that the industrialization of Canada and the discovery and development of its resources are going on at the same time.
At the present time Canada is in approximately the same stage of development as the United States were at the end of the Civil War, but it is in possession of the scientific knowledge and tools of the twentieth century. That is an advantage over the position of the United States at that time. We are able, because of this, to go ahead more rapidly and to forego costly experiments.
With decades of preparation behind it, Canada has made it possible for its twentieth century prospects to move from the realm of dreams to that of reality.
Over the past ten years, Canada has made giant strides. World war II gave us a push along the road to industrialization, and postwar demands have maintained our economy at a high level.
The people of Canada have so well explored our forests, prospected our underground resources, cultivated our plains and constructed hydro electric power stations to move our industrial machinery that this country is now among the foremost providers of the world's needs.
May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to ask the Postmaster General (Mr. Lapointe) to

consider the advisability of building post offices in Dorval and Vilie LaSalle, two municipalities that have made great progress in the past few years and which are about to obtain their civic incorporation. I should like the minister to have plans prepared with a view to having post offices built in these municipalities within a year or two.
In the speech he made in this house on March 30 last, the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Perron) stated that federal-provincial agreements were not appreciated and that no provincial premier had accepted them. That is quite natural. When a child is taken to the store by his parents and keeps asking them for this or that, the father agrees only when he can do so and when his budget allows it.
The federal government spends a great deal of money in the provinces in the form of old age pensions, family allowances, pensions to the blind, health assistance. These considerable sums of money are given to the provinces out of the money collected by the federal government.
Projects undertaken by the federal government, such as the St. Lawrence seaway and the setting-up of a radio and television network across the country, help the provinces. In other words, the federal government spends in the provinces of the country and in proportion to their needs part of the money which it receives from the general tax so that everyone may benefit from the wealth of Canada.
(Text):
There is another matter on which I desire to speak, since I have as many as 400 constituents who are interested as employees of the British Rubber Company Limited, located in Lachine. This firm manufactures rubber footwear for winter, and summer canvas footwear. Before the war this industry enjoyed a substantial export business and did very well in the local market, but during the last few years the export business has been eliminated and imports from foreign nations have taken away 53 per cent of the Canadian market in canvas shoes and 15 per cent of the domestic waterproof shoe market. These imports come largely from Hong Kong and Japan where salaries are very low in comparison with the average of $1.45 an hour paid to Canadian workers. The solution, to my mind, is to place imports on some restricted basis, as it would be impossible to lower wages and the standard of living to the level of workers of the countries just mentioned. This will help to keep the industry operating pending developments. A brief of the manufactures was presented to
The Budget-Mr. Balcer the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) in June last, and more recently, the labour unions feel just as strongly as management does that the situation will have to be corrected if the industry is not to be wiped out.
The Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) met with the representatives of the labour unions and it was finally agreed to form a committee composed of the representatives of the departments of labour, trade and commerce and finance to join with representatives of the unions and management in order to seek methods of saving this industry. I sincerely hope that favourable progress will be made before the end of this session in order that we may study the recommendations of this committee and take whatever action is necessary during this session to permit the manufacturers to prepare their plans in time for next winter.
I wish to thank the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) for the improvement which is being made by the widening of the canal bridge at sixth avenue, Lachine. The present bridge, which was built over 60 years ago, no longer complies with the present heavy traffic requirements and therefore the improvement is badly needed. The widening of the bridge will improve conditions for pedestrians and traffic at that point.
Another thing for which I and the public of Lachine and Vilie St. Pierre will be thankful to the Minister of Transport is his help in bringing about a change in the exit of the sorting yard contemplated to be built at Cote de Liesse by the Canadian National Railways, the exit of which was to be in a residential district of Lachine. The public of Vilie St. Pierre will benefit to a great extent through the alleviation of its traffic problems and the removal of a dangerous spot where many fatalities have occurred in the past. This improvement will be made through the reallocation of the actual railway line.
The suggestions I have just made are offered in a spirit of co-operation with a view to improving the complex administration of government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate, I want to deal briefly with a certain report which has just been released by the dominion bureau of statistics, a report which is of interest to everyone concerned with the economic independence of Canada. I mean the report entitled: "The Canadian International Investment Position 1926-1954". It is a report which shows fantastic figures in respect of U.S. capital investments in Canada.
2826	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Balcer
It says for instance that in 1953 United States capital controlled 55 per cent of mines, oil industries and refining plants in Canada. It shows also that Americans own 43 per cent of the whole amount of capital invested in our manufactures. It shows that from 1948 to 1953, American holdings in Canadian mines and oil refining plants have increased from 37 to 55 per cent, and their holdings in our manufactures have increased from 38 to 43 per cent.
From 1946 to 1955, U.S. capital investments in Canada have grown from $5 billions to $9,600 millions.
The report also reveals that nearly $7 billion 500 million was made up of capital invested in foreign owned companies.
These figures will undoubtedly create worry in several quarters. What is happening before our very eyes is nothing less than economic invasion by our neighbours to the south. It is all the more disturbing when we see that our provincial governments, our municipalities, our chambers of commerce are doing all they can to bring about the establishment of new industries in their own provinces and municipalities in order to create jobs for Canadian workers. And every true Canadian wishes to see our country develop as rapidly as possible.
On the other hand, we can well wonder if the time has not come to ask ourselves what is going on, and whether that invasion by American capital, through our present legislation, is not becoming a serious threat to Canada's economic independence. That danger is even greater as is often the case when American companies come here to establish subsidiary companies of which Canadians cannot get control and in which they cannot even become shareholders.
We can well ask ourselves if this country is not falling into an economic colonialism which may be different from political colonialism but which can be one just the same, and have nefarious effects on the sovereignty and population of Canada.

Shall we keep on sending our unprocessed natural resources to the United States and buy them back in the form of finished products?


There can be no better instance of colonialism than the resolution concerning the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, now before the house, whereby American financiers are requesting this parliament to give them permission to transport natural gas from Alberta to eastern Canada and especially to the United States, and are also asking the Canadian taxpayer to assume part of the costs involved.
Frankly, this is a definite reminder of the treatment which the United States meted out for years to the so-called banana republics of Central America.
The Canadian government has adopted certain attitudes, which have encouraged Americans to act in this way. We have seen the Canadian government, through a crown corporation

in this instance the Canadian National Railways-build a twenty million dollar hotel at public expense and then turn its management over to an American company while all this time we have in this country first class hotels and trained hotel operators. If the Canadian National Railways could not find within their own organization people qualified to manage their hotel in Montreal, which I doubt very much, they only had to turn to the Canadian Pacific Railway which administers hotels such as the Chateau Fron-tenac and the Royal York in a way that is as good as any to be found in other hotels' anywhere in the world.

I will gladly listen to the speech of the hon. member for Gaspe, when his turn comes. Everybody will be glad to listen to him. He will then have an opportunity to answer me if he wishes to do so.
If our government does not resort to all means at its disposal to encourage Canadian capital to play its part in the development of our resources and factories, then, economically, we will merely become a 49th state of the neighbouring republic.
There is no doubt that this invasion of U.S. capital helps us to develop our country, but one wonders if in allowing so much American capital to develop our country, we

are not serving the best interests of the United States rather than our own.
It is quite true that an extraordinary attraction has always existed between our country and the United States. There is an economic north-south attraction which seems just about inevitable between our two countries. Our country is a geographical heresy and the international boundary is purely artificial. And our whole history shows that our country has made its choice for a long long time. Our people, like our ancestors and the past generations, have in turn made up their minds that they want Canada to be a great country, a country independent from the southern republic.
History tells us that Americans first attempted to take a military hold on Canada by attacking us in 1776 and in 1812. Englishspeaking and French-speaking Canadians decided to unite in order to repel this American military invasion.
In 1867, when we gave ourselves a constitution, again our two great races joined in a common front against American invasion once more, but a political invasion that time. That decision on the part of our ancestors entailed economic sacrifices, but they accepted them and resisted. Today we should be inspired by the courage they have shown. Let us' not give away our natural resources, our industries, our manpower to American interests without first taking every possible means of ensuring that Canadian citizens will benefit as much as possible. Through legislation the government should strive to help Canadians to take full or at least partial control of that capital used to develop our natural resources.
Of course, many of our natural resources could not be developed without the help of foreign capital. But it is tragic to think that in many cases those natural resources only serve to improve the standard of living of the American people and not ours.

speechtext:
If American investments in Canada are getting larger for no other reason than the fact that we are giving away our natural resources to American investors so they can develop them by paying low wages, that is not very beneficial to Canada. It is also far from comforting when we see the Canadian government request from parliament the authorization to appropriate $125 million for the construction of a pipe line for the benefit of an American company.
The Budget-Mr. Balcer
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) spoke of Canada's great prosperity; he is so proud of himself and of his colleagues of the government that he did not want to change anything in his budget and he served us exactly the same dish as last year. But one thing he forgot is that salaries of Canadian workers are much lower than those of American workers and that, in general, the standard of living of American workers is higher than that of Canadian workers.
Mr. Speaker, if American capital continues to flow into this country at that rate while the gap remains between the standard of living of the Canadian people and that of the American people, we will be unable to withstand the economic invasion which is going on from day to day across the border. Already many young Canadians emigrate to the United States, because of the higher salaries they can get over there. If we want Canada to remain independent of the republic to the south, we must take steps to give Canadians a better standard of living. If, for instance, we compare the average salary paid in June 1955 in Canadian and American cities, we note that in Detroit, the average salary was $5,057 while at Windsor, which is just opposite, the salary was but $3,692; at Cleveland, the average salary was $4,470 while in Montreal it was only $2,896. The same thing happens almost everywhere. Thus we see that in Seattle the average salary was $4,173 while in Vancouver, which is quite close to Seattle, it was only $3,354.
If we compare the average salary paid in American industries, according to their production and their products, again we find a substantial difference. For instance, in the soft coal industry, the salary paid in the United States is $2.43 an hour while in Canada it is only $1.48. For steel workers, the average rate is $2.24 in the United States and only $1.73 in Canada. In the aluminum industry, the salary paid is $2.14 in the United States while in Canada it is only $1.47 an hour. In copper mines, the rate is $2.12 in the United States and $1.64 here. In packing plants, the rates are $2.05 and $1.52 respectively; in construction, $2.93 and $1.49 only. And so on and so forth all along the line. In the automobile industry, the average salary is $2.20 in the United States and $1.72 only in Canada.
Such a difference between the standards of living in the United States and in Canada
2828	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Balcer should be the main concern of the government. By all available means, the government should strive to eliminate this difference which is responsible for the emigration to the United States of so many young Canadians and which leads to that attitude of defeatism which we are showing towards American capital.
This salary gap is still more striking when one considers the situation of our technicians, our engineers and our specialized workers and becomes particularly impressive when we see that the engineers needed in our industries for the development of our natural resources leave Canada for the United States. Not only do we not train a sufficient number of engineers, but we keep sending many of them to the United States.
We cannot blame those people for migrating to the United States, where, as I have just explained, wages are much higher than in Canada, while the cost of living, at least in respect to many items, is lower than in our country.
The hon. Minister of Finance told us that there was nothing to be changed and that he could come back with the very same budget as that of last year. Well, he has only to look at the prices which prevail in the United States and those which prevail in Canada, and he will find there a target to help him correct his budget.
We can see, for instance, that clothing is much cheaper in the United States than in Canada. The same thing applies to footwear and automobiles.
In Canada, for instance, some people buy a small car which they consider among the lowest-priced available; but then they are told by American garage operators that over there they could have got a Cadillac for the price they paid for their small car.
The same holds true for electrical appliances, television sets, furniture and even foodstuffs, in certain cases.
Another concrete example-and that is a case which comes under federal jurisdiction-[DOT] is that of the cost of cigarettes which are much cheaper in the United States than in Canada.

Let us take for instance personal income tax. A Canadian taxpayer with two dependent children who receives family allowances and whose annual revenue is $3,000 pays $113 in income tax. Yes, that is right: the Canadian taxpayer pays $113 in taxes, whereas the American taxpayer pays only $60.
A father with two dependents, whose annual salary is $4,000 must pay $287, whereas the American taxpayer whose salary is the same only pays $240. The same increase appears at the $5,000 annual salary level. In this case the Canadian taxpayer pays $481 as against $420 for the American.
A Canadian worker who earns $6,000 a year-I should say a superintendent since workers who earn $6,000 a year in this country are rather rare-pays $666 in income tax, as against $600 for his American counterpart.
That is another anomaly we can point out as a target for the efforts of the government and the Minister of Finance if they want to accomplish something in the next twelve months.
We are told that the Canadian citizen enjoys a wonderful social security system. We hear a lot of boasting about family allowances, old age pensions, pensions for the blind, pensions for the veterans of the two world wars, unemployment insurance, etc. Well, there is nothing very original about that system since such social security legislation exists in all the civilized countries of the world. Furthermore, that Canadian legislation loses some of its real value and of its purchasing power from day to day, with the government doing practically nothing to prevent such a situation.
Let us take for instance the case of old age pensions. The bill setting up the pension at $40 a month was passed in 1949. Today,
7 years later, the purchasing power of this $40 pension has been reduced considerably, in fact, it has gone down from $40 in 1949 to $32.29 in 1956.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I again want to direct attention to the predicament in which the farmers in the constituency of Selkirk find themselves. I have heard remarks to the effect that I have made things look worse than they really were. I want to contradict that statement right away. Conditions in Selkirk constituency are really bad and I have not made them look any worse than they really are.
When speaking in the house on a previous occasion I said that there would be people starving in the Selkirk constituency unless something was done to relieve the situation. When I said that people were going to be starving, I did not figure that anybody was going to die because out west they do not let a man die if they can possibly help it. In looking through the dictionary I find that the meaning given for "starve" is to die or suffer from the lack of food, go hungry, keep without or be short of food. These are the things that are taking place in Selkirk today. There is nobody dying but the people are in bad shape. I want hon. members to believe me when I say that is what I meant the last time when I used those words in this house. I did not figure that anybody was going to die but I figured that they were in fairly bad shape and needed attention.
I am going to put on the record one or two letters in order to back up what I am saying and to prove that I am not coming here and speaking just for the sake of speaking. When I rise in this house I do so in order to direct attention to the problems of the people that I represent. I want you to believe me, Mr. Speaker, when I say that. I have no political axe to grind. I am the representative of the people of Selkirk as long as I am here, and their problems will come first with me. This letter that I am going to read is from a man at Washow Bay in my constituency. He writes as follows:
Dear Sir:
I refer to the prairie farm assistance. I live here in this newly-settled country, 9 miles north of Riverton town. Since the last 2 years we received too much rain and thus received little or no crops. So therefore, the P.F.A. has paid to low township land owners, cheques of $200 per year and more. I don't get any. I am in the same township where the other farmers here received it.
[Mr. Habel.l
My land has been broken the same time as theirs and competes with theirs in every way. They had none broken before 1940.
The P.F.A. says we can't get any P.F.A. cheques since we bought our land since 1940. That does not encourage the Manitoba public. In my case we are in extreme need of this assistance, since it has been collected from us in good years.
I have a lame back and cannot work. I have to hitchhike to a doctor or chiropractor for aid and the bills are running too high. The land payments are past due and taxes need paying. We have to pay them this spring or else. I have a wife and 4 children to care for besides myself. We own no new car or unreasonable equipment. Thirty-five acres are broken on this quarter which I did to our own expenses in hope of returns. These last 2 years very little to account for puts us far behind. It would be enough if we got the fair P.F.A. cheques, the same as the rest. It would put us in fair terms again if we could receive this P.F.A. assistance or some kind of relief which we need badly. I ask you kindly, is there something that you can do for us? We do not intend to give up if we don't have to.
I am going to read another one from another part of Selkirk constituency, about 75 miles from there. This one is from Eriksdale and reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am writing you in regard to the payments that have been made to farmers during the month of December 1955, by prairie farm assistance.
As I believe you do know just how hard hit the farmers in the interlake district were hit by excess rainfall causing our land to be completely flooded. Some farmers being luckier than others due to their land being higher, but those of us that have to take the run-off of the higher land really haven't a chance to get on the land.
Now here is the part that is so unfair. P.F.A. has been paid to most of the farmers around here even those that never do cultivate their land. Some have been paid $120 to $200, this to be 60 per cent of their payment. Some do not know what they were being paid for, as they got the large amount of $13 to $14 which surely could not be called assistance. But we were completely left out, we did not get any and as I said before, we are living in the valley of the run-off waters from higher lands. We have 90 acres to crop and for 3 years now have had a total loss, yet expenses are piling up-just trying to get the land seeded only to lose it all.
Now I am asking you to see what can be done about this. Why should we not be paid assistance when practically the whole municipality has received some except I doz. farmers all in one locality. And a fair share, not $200 to some or somewhere about that and others a few dollars which isn't more than a barrel of fuel.
No one knows on what grounds the P.F.A. is making assistance as some do not even expect any have gotten assistance-others know they are entitled to P.F.A. do not receive any.
It would be greatly appreciated if you could help us to get our fair share of P.F.A. as I have mentioned before, if they have paid P.F.A. to some in this district, why just leave a few out.
That is another problem. I am putting these on the record because sometimes I think, when 1 go back home-and I was back home at Easter-that people think I have been sitting down here and have never brought

these complaints to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I am quite sure that the Minister of Agriculture gets from me more letters than he gets from other members in the house, all on the same subject. This one is from Fisher Branch and it reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
I will need some assistance for my complete crop flooded out for 1954-1955. X wrote to P.F.A. in Regina, Sask., but they refuse assistance. They say X bought my land too late after the war. But I had been farming on the other land at Fisher Branch before the war, and they had been collecting on every load that I brought to the elevator.
Try and give me help some way. I have no income, no job out here, and the taxes are behind. I have 72 acres under cultivation but that was a complete loss for 2 years.
This one is from Arborg, in another part of my constituency:
Dear Sir:
I just received a cheque in regard to prairie farm assistance for $97.50.
I had 144 acres summerfallowed and it comes up to about 65* an acre. The farmers were asking $2.50, but then since it was refused they asked at least $1.25.
How much help can a cheque like this be when we have to buy feed, seed, fertilizer and fuel?
What about taxes? It is just terrible the way the farmers are treated. We havn't received much help just these past 2 years when we were flooded out, and now we get such a miserable aid.
The best solution would be to quit this darn farming and hit for the city.
When we sell something, eggs, hogs or cattle, its just a disgrace. This year we have to buy feed at the elevator for poultry, cattle, hogs, and they charge us 81 cents a bushel for oats. There is no dockage, and no question of damp or tough. But what did we get when we were able to sell? Forty cents a bushel, and, of course, dockage, and if it wasn't damp it was tough.
Just how will the farmer survive? When he has to buy something, he sure pays for it too.
I have two boys 12 and 13, and they already don't want to hear anything about making a career of farming.
I hope you can. point up a few things to the Liberals. What the farmers are up against, and get more assistance-this at least for spring work.
It sure burns one up how they expect the farmer to work for nothing-as that is exactly what he is doing now.
To think Canada is so rich in food, and here we farmers cannot afford to buy fruit and vegetables in winter for our kids.
Hoping this will give you an idea of our situation. Here is a letter from Fisher Branch, Manitoba:
As you are well aware of the conditions on the farms in this area in the last few years, most of farmers are in a very bad shape financially due mainly to crop failures. And now the P.F.A.A. has turned down some of us, others are getting 75 cents per acre, which of course is very little. We don't know how they figure out but the crop was so bad in this township and other townships here that it certainly did not average 4 bushels to the acre as only an odd spot in some higher field had a bit of crop on it and all the rest was flooded out or even could not be seeded because of flooding. We never asked for assistance from anyone
The Budget-Mr. Bryce when we had fair crops, but now we don't know what the farmers around here are going to do this spring-they need seed and fuel for their tractors and repairs, etc. Not mentioning their debts that are long overdue.
Now, Mr. Bryce, we know there are many others like us writing you but we don't see where else we can go. Our provincial government doesn't want to hear about our troubles, sometimes they are nice enough to say they are going to look into the matter and that is how far it gets.
You will recall in the war years the government paid the farmers in Canada $4.00 per acre if they did not seed wheat on those acres and that cost this country a lot of money. But now this crop failure is only a very small area in Canada in the interlake area that was flooded out, so certainly our government can assist these poor people this time.
We are leaving this to your kind consideration.
I received a copy of a resolution from the Fisher Branch Manitoba Farmers' Union, Local 16, which reads as follows:
Whereas the farmers who bought land from the government after 1940 are not able to participate in the P.F.A.A. assistance-and as these farmers contribute into this fund when they deliver grain to any elevator-and as these farmers are in a desperate need of assistance in this area
Be it Resolved: That we urge the government to consider these needy fellows and bring them into the P.F.A.A. program so they may participate in the assistance along with the other farmers.
Now, on March 15 I asked the Minister of Agriculture a question, reported on page 2159 of Hansard for that date, as follows:
Can the minister inform the house when he expects to bring before the house the amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and what they will cover?
The minister answered me the same day, and this was his answer:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that we made rather material amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act last session. When we were preparing legislation for this session or the items upon which legislation might be required, we were having considerable difficulty in the administration of the amendments which were made last year. We therefore made provision for the possibility of bringing in amending legislation. However, I am now informed that, with greater experience in the administration, the difficulties have become less and less, and I am not sure that it will be necessary to bring down legislation.
I had hoped that some temporary amendments would be brought in to help the farmers who have not been able to participate in P.F.A.A. I still do not think it is right or proper for the government to collect 1 per cent from farmers who can never expect to derive any benefits from that fund, and especially the man who is dependent entirely on his farm. I do not know the law as well as I should like, but it seems to me it must be an injustice to collect a tax of 1 per cent and refuse the farmers any benefit from it.
The minister has explained that when the provincial government took over crown lands in Manitoba it was made quite clear to that
2832	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Bryce government that the federal government would not be responsible for any assistance or aid at any time. Now, I took that up with the Hon. Mr. Robertson, the Manitoba minister of agriculture, last year, and he claimed that he knew nothing at all about such an arrangement being made and he would not have anything to do with it. According to Hansard of June 21, 1955, the Minister of Agriculture when speaking on his estimates said that approximately $300,000 had been collected from people who, according to the provisions of the act, could never participate in any of the benefits. This $300,000 had been collected from people who were on crown lands. These farmers are not receiving P.F.A.A. aid because the act says they are not to get it.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is looking at me and I venture to say he believes there is something wrong with my argument. I certainly do not know the law, but 1 per cent of the proceeds of every load of grain the farmer delivers to the elevator goes into the consolidated revenue fund of this country. The act says that if he bought his land from the government after 1940 he cannot participate in any benefits. Then, why take the money from him? I wonder if the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture could not take that $300,000-I was going to say obtained under false pretenses, and it is very nearly that- and give some of it back to these fellows.
It seems so ridiculous when you have a section of land consisting of four quarters and three fellows who own three quarters get $200 each because their crops have been drowned out for two years, but the other fellow whose crop has also been drowned out gets nothing because he bought his land after they bought theirs. If you analyse the thing you will find that perhaps the fellow who bought his land after 1940 had it broken and in cultivation before the other fellows had theirs. That is the position today. If the government would take some of that $300,000 and divide it among those fellows who are in need it would be of great help to them. They have paid into the fund; they have the same kind of land as the other settlers but the purchase date is different. People who have been able to participate in the benefits of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act find it hard enough to get along, and with no help it is so much worse.
I do not want to repeat my arguments. I do not believe in repeating a thing for some other body's benefit. If they do not listen to me the first time I make the argument they will not listen to it a second time. Why can a government collect a tax and refuse the benefits? I wonder whether the minister has
IMr. Bryce.]

ever had a legal opinion to see whether they really can do that? A lot of things go through the Exchequer Court for legal opinions that are not as worthy as this, because it would protect many farmers. I hope the minister will consider this matter of paying part of the $300,000 to the people on crown land who have paid into the fund.
One other thing that concerns the farmers in the Selkirk constituency is getting seed and feed this spring. After losing their crops for two years running, a very large percentage of the farmers have no seed or feed left. There are many fortunate farmers in the constituency of Selkirk because we have some very wealthy people there who have been in the farming business for a long time and who have weathered the storm in good years and bad years right along. It will not affect them. They will come up shining in the spring and they have money to take care of their operations. I am thinking of the boys who were sent overseas. They are not in the same position. They are still paying for their land. They are struggling to get along. These are the fellows who are going to be hard hit, the younger generation. I know the situation and I do hope that they will do a little better than they have been doing. It is the rising generation, the 25 and 30-year olds, the men and women of tomorrow, who are concerned. If you make it difficult for them they will go back to the cities and agriculture will be the loser. This is air agricultural country, and it is the young people who are to carry on, not old fellows like me.
About a month ago a survey was taken in Fisher Branch, Poplarfield and Chatfield districts. Those districts have no seed or feed. A survey was taken to see how much they need in the Fisher Branch district. Ninety-three farmers were consulted. They need 8,500 bushels of oats, 3,800 bushels of barley, 5,400 bushels of wheat and 600 bushels of flax. In the Poplarfield district there were 51 farmers canvassed. They need 9,000 bushels of oats, 1,155 bushels of barley, and 2,000 bushels of oats. In Chatfield, 12 farmers were canvassed. They need 755 bushels of oats, 200 bushels of barley and 65 bushels of wheat. As near as I can estimate there is a population of about 700 in these three districts. If they could get seed it would lie of tremendous benefit to them.
Some farmers have written letters to me requesting that I take this up. Some of them have said: "If the government will only give us this seed we shall take the seed back to them in the elevator in the fall, but do not ask us to pay interest because we are deep enough in the hole now." They would pay back bushel for bushel in the fall for the seed borrowed. What the farmers do not

want to do is to go to the municipality and borrow at 6 per cent. This only puts the farmer deeper in debt. I hope the government will make it possible for farmers to get seed this way should they so desire it.
I have received a copy of a brief presented to the municipality of St. Andrews in Selkirk constituency by the farmers union at Petersfield and Clandeboye. I am not going to read the whole of it. It shows the trend of thought and what they are trying to do. The brief reads in part as follows:
It is evident that there are a number of farmers who, due to crop failure, have been forced to seek other sources of income in order to maintain their livelihood. These farmers are not eligible for payment under the regulations of the act. We realize that you cannot do much about the regulations of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, as it comes under the jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament, but we do feel that your council, being the first phase of local government, does have certain powers and could make recommendations that would be of assistance in solving some of our agricultural problems.
The final point that we wish to discuss with you is the seed grain and farm fuel assistance through the legislation available under the seed, fuel and fodder act of Manitoba. It is apparent that many of our farmers will require assistance if they are going to get any crop this year. The financial situation being what it is, many will not be able to purchase seed and fuel requirements this spring. We therefore wish to request the council's immediate consideration of assistance through seed, fuel and fodder act.
We believe that the support of your council is necessary before the government will take an interest in this issue. We wish to impress upon you that we cannot minimize the danger that exists in the Interlake area for 1956. The moisture condition of the soil last fall was not as dry as some people would like us to believe. When we realize that it was not possible to work some of the land until late summer and when we consider the heavy snowfall this winter, it is obvious that many of our farmers may be hard hit again. Should this happen, it will mean that some farms will have been flooded for four years in succession.
I presented a petition this afternoon on behalf of 2,511 petitioners. Since I did that this afternoon I have received in the mail another 125 signatures, which brings the total up to 2,636. It deals with the advisability of declaring the flooded Assiniboine river valley and the interlake area a disaster area.
The second section asks for the granting of financial assistance on the basis of $5 per productive acre flooded during the 1955 crop year, which would assist them to maintain their farm homes and to put in a crop this coming spring.
This petition brings the plight of the farmers in the flooded Assiniboine river valley and the Interlake area of the province of Manitoba before the government again. In the majority of cases, farmers have suffered from flooding for the last two or three years. In such a large area as the Interlake country, from the Assiniboine river north, a great
The Budget-Mr. Bryce many different phases of agriculture are in operation. In some places it is grain, in some places it is cattle and in other places it is mixed farming. If you take the districts of St. Laurent, Oak Point, Lundar and that part of the country bordering on Lake Manitoba, cattle raising or beef production is how the farmers make their livelihood. The P.F.A.A. has never been of any benefit to them. However, their pastures both tame and wild have been flooded and they have suffered a great deal. Last year, the second year of flooding, left them with no place to pasture their cattle and many of the farmers have had to dispose of their cattle as feeders when with good pasture they could have finished the cattle and realized a much better price.
The mixed farmer has had similar problems. He has been short of pasture and has not been able to grow any feed. This has cut down his cream production and has left him short of cash with which to carry on. I have already dealt with the man who grows grain.
As I said before, this petition endeavours to get the government to look at the situation and see what can be done. An arrangement like this based on productive acreage would be of assistance to the cattlemen, the beef producers, the mixed farmers and the grain farmers.
When I was home at Easter I was approached by a farmer who told me that he had been forbidden to use his tractor until he makes a further payment. Another farmer has written to tell me that action was commenced against him by filing a statement of claim in the county court for a debt. Surely some arrangement can be made to ask creditors to wait until the farmers get a crop.
My time is just about up but in the time left at my disposal I would like to go into the debt situation. I know from my visit to my home last week that not only one or two but a great many people are in difficulties. I would like now to quote from the submission made to the government this year by the interprovincial farm union council. I have just about three minutes left and I think I can deal with it in that length of time. I shall read from page 20 of the submission, the paragraph under the heading "Debt Adjustment Laws", which says:
The drastic fluctuation in farm income in Canada makes it very difficult at times for even the most efficient farmer to meet his liabilities as they come due. When that happens the farmer is faced with the prospect of being sued and having a judgment against him, or having his mortgage foreclosed or his agreement for sale cancelled, and in either case of losing his land.
There are some creditors who deal leniently with their farm debtors and help them over their difficulties, but some refuse to be influenced by these considerations and insist on strict enforcement of their contracts. The result is that many hardworking farmers are being driven from their land-

The Budget-Mr. Robertson a situation which clearly is against not only the interest of the individual concerned but of the country as a whole.
To meet this situation, debt adjustment laws have been placed on the statute books from time to time in the various provinces, for the protection of farm debtors who, because of circumstances beyond their control, became involved in financial difficulties. However the history of this type of provincial legislation has been that the courts have always held such laws to be invalid, because under the British North America Act the right to legislate with respect to bankruptcy and insolvency was designated to the Canadian parliament. The most recent example along this line is the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, delivered on November 15, 1955, which declared the Moratorium Act of Saskatchewan to be ultra vires.
In the depression years of the thirties, parliament did legislate to protect farmers who could not discharge their obligations, by passing the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act-a most useful statute a few years ago, but of practically no use just now, at a time when a similar up-to-date law is perhaps more needed than ever.
Therefore, we suggest that efforts should be made at this time by the government to have legislation passed creating a board empowered to give protection to unfortunate farmers against being forced into bankruptcy.
I support that submission. I think the recommendations it outlines are necessary and I hope my remarks will be given some consideration.
