subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget as presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) was realistic, responsible and encouraging. It is realistic because in view of high expenditures we could not expect more reductions in taxation. It is responsible because it is prudent in prosperous times to pay our way and have a balanced budget. It is encouraging because of the minister's forecast of continued or even expanded development in our economy for the coming year.
It was a source of great satisfaction to me, Mr. Speaker, to hear the review of our economic prospects as given by the Minister of Finance. He told us of the high production, of the high employment and of the high income in Canada; in fact, these were at an all-time high for the last year. He predicted there would be a total national production of $28 billion for the coming fiscal year. Other important Canadians agree with the Minister of Finance and I would like to quote from the Ottawa Citizen of February 2, 1956, an opinion expressed by the president of Imperial Oil Limited, Mr. J. R. White. This is headed, "Canada producing equivalent of country with 100 million people."
The report reads:
Canada, in terms of what she produces, is the equivalent of a country of 100 million people rather than 16 million, J. R. White, president of Imperial Oil Limited, said Monday night in an address to the Halifax board of trade.

The figures, he said, reflect the fact that in terms of the world's production Canada ranks six times greater than her population.
Looking ahead, Mr. White predicted for 1980:
A population of 25 million, nearly 60 per cent more than now.
A total gross dollar volume of business nearly 24 times that of today.
Two-thirds more homes, more than 7 million passenger automobiles compared with today's 24 million and twice as many farm tractors.
Discoveries of up to 30 billion barrels of oil, compared with current known reserves of 3 billion -and an investment of up to $22 billion, or more than seven times the ?3 billion already invested in oil development.
One is sometimes staggered by the predictions made for the development of our country, but I venture to say that within the next 20 or 30 years, as our country develops, many of these predictions will have been found to be far too low. Fortunately the cost of living during this period has remained relatively stable so that our people have enjoyed a higher level in their standard of living than ever before. As the minister pointed out, however, some sections of our economy did not share in this general prosperity. The minister mentioned agriculture as an example and I would like to add to that the textile industry. I believe that the government should give serious consideration to the position of the textile industry and give it all the relief it can under present circumstances. I will have more to say concerning agriculture later on in my speech.
The government is certainly consistent in its finance policy. When he budgets for a surplus of $125 million the minister is simply following the wise example laid down by previous finance ministers. Ever since the war and up until last year the Liberal government has been budgeting for surpluses because they believe that in periods of prosperity we should pay our way and balance our budget. However, last year when conditions were less encouraging the minister did not hesitate to budget for a deficit and I think the wisdom of his decision has been more than substantiated at the present time.
I do not believe that many people in Canada expected a tax reduction because they are aware that our estimates this year indicate an expenditure of nearly $4-75 billion. In addition to this the government has indicated that it is willing to support a health insurance scheme costing $200 million a year.
In addition again there will be the expenditure on the Trans-Canada pipe line and I hope that before long this parliament will pass the necessary legislation because I believe that this pipe line is necessary for the further development of this country. I hope that there will be no unnecessary delay in making this feasible in our country. It has

been indicated by the opposition groups that they will likely oppose the present suggestion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Of course we acknowledge their right to do so, but I would suggest to them that once they have placed their position on the record there will be nothing but delay gained by discussing the matter at any length. I for one am prepared to be found in the camp of this government and I support the measure as laid out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I also know that the government of the province of Ontario supports this procedure.
There were few tariff changes in the budget presented by the minister, but I was glad to see that what tariff changes there were were changes that will help agriculture. They cover repair parts for farm machinery, equipment for artificial breeding units and other items for use on the farm.
I should like to mention briefly the fact that the government is going to spend another $9 million in the form of further aid under the Colombo plan and the United Nations technical assistance program. I believe that these [DOT] programs have the wholehearted support of the vast majority of the Canadian people and that they are making a real contribution to peace in this world.
I should like to speak for a few minutes about federal-provincial relations, and in this connection I should like to pay tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) for their efforts to bring about agreement in this matter. During the past year we have had four meetings of premiers as well as conferences of ministers on other occasions. They have dealt with the following questions: Unemployment insurance, hospital insurance, the trans-Canada highway and fiscal relations.
We all know that the federal government has made a proposal to the provincial government's under which they would be prepared to assume 50 per cent of the cost of unemployment assistance whenever the number of people on relief in a province rises above a certain nominal figure. I know that the federal government proposals have few if any limitations except this fact. They do not ask whether a person is employable and there is no limit placed on the amount which a province or municipality may grant to these persons if they are in need. That is left entirely to the province. I think this is another indication of the good will of the federal government in arriving at a reasonable agreement on this matter.
I have indicated also that the federal government have made proposals regarding hospital insurance which if accepted by all the provinces of Canada will require $200 million
The Budget-Mr. Robertson a year from the federal treasury. I want to say at once that I support wholeheartedly a program of hospital insurance because I believe there are many people in Canada who cannot afford proper hospital treatment. This need is very great indeed. In saying that I speak from my experience as a medical practitioner in the province of Ontario.
Further, the federal government has also made a liberal proposition to the provinces in connection with building the trans-Canada highway. We in this parliament will be considering this legislation at some future time.
I come now to fiscal relations which after all is the most important feature of federal-provincial relations. I believe that in a federal state where inequalities exist one duty of the federal government is to minimize such inequalities. The present tax rental agreements have sought to accomplish this, and in my opinion they have done so. Our objective has been to share with the provinces our direct taxation revenue in order to produce equity and stability in the revenues of the provinces, to eliminate the duplication of direct taxation and bring about the simplification of our tax laws. 1 submit that these tax rental agreements have accomplished these objectives.
In dealing with this matter I think we must have in mind three important factors. One is that the various provincial governments have very different degrees and types of tax potential. Second, while the costs of various services vary in the different provinces they do not vary as greatly as do the tax potentials. Third, with the development of large-scale enterprises operating on a nation-wide basis usually the income and profits of these industries which are earned in all the provinces of Canada can be taxed effectively only in the province in which the head office is located, which is generally either in the province of Quebec or in the province of Ontario.
According to the speech made by the minister when presenting his budget, if the proposals recently made to the provinces were applied to the present tax rate they would yield them a total of $640 million, whereas the tax rental agreements which were previously in effect yielded $531 million. This is an increased offer by the federal government of over $109 million. In my opinion that is a most generous offer, bearing in mind the tremendous responsibility of the federal government. We have been spending and must continue for some time to spend nearly $2,000 million on national defence.
The federal government has already relieved the provinces of huge responsibilities. Consider for a moment what we have done in

The Budget-Mr. Robertson the way of social security which under our constitution is a provincial responsibility. We pay the full amount of family allowances and of old age security and we share with the provinces the cost of old age assistance, allowances for the blind and disabled persons' allowances. The federal government has made an offer to share with the provinces the cost of unemployment assistance and to bear half the cost of a hospital insurance scheme. Surely the federal government has done what any reasonable person would ask it to do in this regard.
I believe that the residents of the wealthier provinces must not-nor do I believe they do -object to assistance to the less wealthy provinces. Only in this manner can confederation develop in the spirit of unity and cooperation. I believe that first of all we are Canadians. While we wish to see every province have what revenue it requires for its essential purposes, nevertheless we must have a broader vision and do what is best for the nation as a whole.
In this regard I should like to quote, from the Financial Times of March 23, 1956, an article written by the celebrated correspondent Tempus. It is headed:
Government Under Fire For Saving the Taxpayers' Money.
It states:
You remember how Stalin has tried to rewrite history. Well, the Tory press of Canada has attempted the same thing in commenting on the recent provincial-federal conference. The 1956 federal-provincial conference was George Orwell's "1984" again.
All the Prime Minister tried to do was to save the Canadian taxpayer money.
For doing that, he was given the works; and so was the finance minister Walter Harris.
Here is what happened; Prime Minister St. Laurent chose to hold on to the taxpayers' money against ten provincial panhandlers. Never, even in some Arabian Night story, have such elegant "hand it over" fellows shown up here on the hill to grab money. If they had gotten their way Canada would have been bankrupt for years.
Rather cleverly, and with insidious deviousness, the provincial premiers have tried to show themselves as merely wanting to get their own money back. Well, if everybody had got his own way, the federal government would have had no money for any public business, welfare or otherwise.
St. Laurent had already given the provincial premiers a take it or leave it dictum. They could come to Ottawa, if they liked. But-they were not going to get any extra money. They had had enough . . .
The Prime Minister promised them nothing. The provincial premiers came because it was a glorious toot for them. Let not the taxpayers be fooled. The provincial premiers all love to come to Ottawa on expense account. Then they get enough anti-Ottawa ammunition to last them half a year. Besides a couple of them figure they acquired enough material for a political platform to carry them into power on a provincial election. But more than one such anti-Ottawa platform has turned out to be a political hearse!

So now the provincial apologists call the St. Laurent government deceptive. One of the premiers wanted to gouge the federal treasury for a cool $100 million. It used to be the criterion of political excellence if you could grab enough post offices; you were a great success. Now the test of provincial excellence is to take from the federal treasury the maximum amount of hard cash.
There is only one set of taxpayers. The provinces keep forgetting that.
I believe that editorial was written in a somewhat jovial vein, but I suggest there is great food for thought for the Canadian taxpayer in that article. I would ask the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the government to continue their efforts to build a stronger and even more united Canada.
There is another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance. I refer to the grants to the municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal property within the municipalities. I would congratulate the government on the steps it has taken in this matter. The Municipal Grants Act was enacted on June 30, 1951. Very briefly I might point out that there are three kinds of grants; first, the annual grants in lieu of real property taxes; second, transitional grants which afford relief to the municipalities for-loss of taxes where taxable property has been acquired by the federal government after December 31, 1948; third, grants in lieu of special assessments for local improvements.
I believe that in the municipalities where these grants are functioning there is general satisfaction with what the government has done in this matter. As most hon. members know, these grants are paid to municipalities only when there is abnormal concentration of federal property within their boundaries. At first it was paid to municipalities that had over 4 per cent of federal property as compared with the total value of taxable and federal property in the municipalities. Last year the minister reported to this house that 48 municipalities in Canada were sharing in the benefits of that legislation. At that time he introduced legislation which broadened the base so a larger number of municipalities could qualify. This was done by reducing the minimum percentage factor from 4 per cent to 2 per cent; by relating the grant to the ratio of federal property to taxable property only, instead of the ratio of the federal property to taxable and federal property combined; and, third, by the removal of the 75 per cent factor. At the present time the grants are calculated at the full property tax rates.
In my opinion, the government might very well give consideration to paying taxes on federal property in all municipalities. I do not believe this would mean a terrific increase in cost, because the municipalities where the heavy concentration of federal property does exist are already receiving by far the greater

proportion of their normal taxes. However, I believe that other municipalities, particularly those which are just under the 2 per cent, should be given further consideration. In my opinion, of course, the provincial governments should do likewise; but I believe that if the federal government would give leadership in this regard, the provinces would soon follow suit. The provinces, it is true, do make generous grants for education, for road building, for welfare and other purposes, but these grants are paid irrespective of any provincial property in the municipality and cannot be considered grants in lieu of taxation.
I should like to put on the record some assessment facts concerning my own town of Cobourg. I know there is a total taxable assessment of $9,140,000. The federal and provincial property in that town consists of $2,373,000 federal and $356,000 provincial, making a total for federal and provincial property of $2,729,365. When we add to that other exempt property in the town, we find that there is a total property exemption of over $5 million and a total taxable assessment of only $9,140,000. I must, however, thank the government for its very liberal grant to the town of Cobourg in lieu of taxes. As I have indicated, we have federal property in that municipality of over $2,373,000. This is due to the fact that the large No. 26 central ordnance depot is located in this area. The grant to the town of Cobourg amounts to just under $100,000, which, in a total budget of just over $700,000, is a very considerable sum.
We hear much of the need for further assistance to the municipalities, and I believe the provincial and federal governments can provide very necessary assistance to the municipalities by paying their full taxes wherever this property exists.
Now I come to the last subject I wish to discuss today, namely the situation of agriculture in our country. Earlier in my remarks I indicated that I wished to discuss this problem at some length. The Minister of Finance in his budget address, and the Minister of Agriculture have already told this house that agriculture is not sharing fully in the general prosperity of this country. As the representative of a riding half of whose citizens follow agriculture, I am naturally concerned with the fact that farm income has not kept pace with income in other industries in our economy. Agriculture, for a period up to 1951 enjoyed a period of great prosperity, 1 think the greatest in its history. However, since that time farm income has declined. Not only has the farm income declined but the expenses of farm operation have actually
The Budget-Mr. Robertson increased. I am told that the costs of farm operation are 2 per cent higher today than they were in 1951.
I believe that the prosperity of our agricultural citizens must be a primary concern of any government. I would ask this government to look very carefully into the situation to see whether anything more can be done to aid the farmers with their present problems. However, I must pay tribute to the policies of this government, which I believe have been of great aid to agriculture over the years.
I place first among these the farm price support policy and I should like to deal with this matter later in my remarks. However, in addition to that we have paid subsidies on various agricultural products. We pay a large part of the transportation cost of feed grain to eastern Canada. We have premiums for higher grades on many of our products. We are spending money on research in order to learn how to deal with various agricultural problems. We have provided credit for farmers in various ways. Hence, Mr. Speaker,
I think this government has done much for our agricultural citizens.
I support wholeheartedly the farm price support policy of this government because I believe it has made a real contribution to stabilizing, to some extent at least, farm income in this country, thereby making a real contribution to the economy of Canada as a whole. The purpose of the farm price support policy, as I understand it, is to make sure that the farmers receive a reasonable return during periods of high production and to prevent the consumer being charged an unreasonable amount during periods of low production.
I think a classic example of how this policy has worked is the butter situation as we have seen it develop in this country over the last 10 years. Prior to 1949 the government had been supporting butter at 58 cents a pound. In 1949 this support price was lowered to 53 cents per pound. Immediately production was decreased. In 1950 and 1951 we had to import some 22 million pounds of butter from New Zealand. In February of 1951 the consumer in Canada was paying 90 cents a pound for butter. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this proves very well indeed the high value of our farm price support policy.
I would ask the government, through the Minister of Agriculture, for the continuation of all the present floor prices, because I feel they are vital not only for agriculture but for the prosperity of the country as a whole. I believe that the citizens living in the cities should be somewhat better informed of the purpose of these farm price support measures because I think the farmer, the businessman
2838	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Robertson and the wage earner are each dependent on the prosperity of the other. National economic policy, if it is to succeed, can neglect neither agriculture nor the maintenance of high industrial income and employment. We must seek to obtain for the farm family a standard of living comparable with that enjoyed by workers in other industries.
At the present time the hog situation is not too satisfactory. In reading the paper today I notice that hogs have dropped to the floor price of $23 per hundredweight, although I doubt whether as yet the government has had to purchase any of these hogs.
I believe the reason for this depression in the hog industry is the terrific production which took place in Canada last year as compared with that in previous years. We are fortunate, however, that there has been such an increased consumption on the domestic market, and that we have been able to export some of our hog products to the United States. I think we should certainly continue this support price of $23 per hundredweight for hogs, I think the Minister of Agriculture could very well give consideration to having increased premiums for grade A hogs.
I believe this suggestion was put forward yesterday by the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Bennett). To me it is a means of assisting the farm producer, and more particularly of ensuring a high quality in our hog products, something which will make it much easier for us to export to the United States, as they desire this type of bacon. We should also keep in mind the British market, should dollars become more available in that country.
I have already indicated that the butter policy of this government meets with my wholehearted approval. I am pleased that we are able to get rid of some of our surplus in export markets, and I hope the government will endeavour to do more of this in the future. If we are able to export even a small percentage of our butter we shall have no need to worry about the disposal of the remainder of the butter produced in our country.
I believe the success of the government's policy in this regard is shown by the fact that the farmer's share of the retail price of butter increased from 60 per cent in 1939 to 78 per cent in 1955. Possibly this fact explains the attitude of the National Dairy Council, composed as it is for the most part of the large dairies of Canada, in opposing the government's present policy on the marketing of butter. We are noticing an increased domestic consumption of butter and cheese in Canada, and I have been informed that


there is every hope that this year the production and consumption of butter will be more in balance.
I would also ask the government to restrict the importation of New Zealand cheese into Canada. If we can arrange it, I think it would be as well not to have any New Zealand cheese coming into Canada, though in saying this I believe our decision must be made in the light of the general international trade picture. We certainly must realize that international trade is a two-way street and that we cannot expect only to export as we certainly do not want to return to the Canada-first policy of the Bennett government which was so disastrous to the Canadian farmer.
I believe the farmers themselves recognize this fact. I should like to read from a statement of policy by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture published in January, 1955. It reads as follows:
Whatever protection to the farmer from import competition may be found necessary, it must be provided in such a manner that the legitimate interests of consumers are protected. Moreover, Canada's and the farmers' fundamental dependence on a healthy and expanding foreign trade must be recognized and taken into account.
There is another matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance. I would ask for a reconsideration of the tariff which is imposed on turkeys coming into this country. As hon. members know, there are three types of turkeys, live, dressed and eviscerated, and the large proportion of the trade both ways is in eviscerated turkeys. At the present time the Canadian tariff is 12-5 per cent ad valorem on each of these classes of turkeys. On live turkeys this Canadian tariff amounts to 4 cents per pound, whereas the United States duty is 2 cents per pound. On dressed turkeys we have the 12-5 per cent ad valorem which I believe amounts to about
4	cents per pound, whereas the United States tariff is 10 cents per pound. Then in the field of eviscerated turkeys, in which I am particularly interested, we know that our duty is 12-5 per cent whereas the United States tariff is 12-5 per cent with a minimum of 5 cents per pound.
I think that in Canada we could very well have the tariff on the importation of turkeys the same as that of the United States, namely that we should have a minimum of
5	cents per pound. If production in turkeys is high in the United States and the price falls, then our protection may go down as low as 3 cents a pound. Of course the reverse is true; if prices go up in the United States, then our tariff will increase and may be as high as 6 cents per pound. However,
I think we could very well have a minimum of 5 cents a pound on these turkeys.
APRIL n. 1956
I should like also to state that in my opinion floor prices for agricultural products should be employed almost always on a national scale. I believe the government acted wisely in refusing the request of the Nova Scotia apple producer for assistance similar to what he enjoyed in past years, and offering instead assistance of 1 cent per pound available to all provinces in Canada. I do not believe it is equitable for the government to pay assistance to one province on a product which cannot be sold profitably in another part of Canada.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak quite briefly on marketing legislation for farmers. I believe that herein lies the solution to many of the problems which are facing agriculture today. We know that some of our provincial marketing schemes are to be considered by the courts to see if they have legal authority to continue. I believe that all governments should make sure these schemes have the required authority and if necessary legislation should be introduced to make the marketing schemes in Canada fully legal. I believe that to farmers marketing legislation is as important as the right to organize in unions is to labour, and all governments should take the necessary steps to see that this is properly handled.
I have had the pleasure of attending many meetings of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in my riding. More recently farm union clubs are being organized, and I hope I shall have the pleasure of meeting with these farm representatives on an early occasion. I believe these organizations are vital to the welfare of the farmer, and that through them much can be done to solve the problems of agriculture. I ask for the continued interest of this government on all problems affecting the welfare of agriculture.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to some of your remarks regarding whether or not people were reading speeches. I know that as a new member speaking for the first time I am allowed certain privileges. As I was sitting here looking at what I have in front of me I thought if you asked me the direct question, "Are you reading your speech?", I just do not know how I could honestly answer you. I have not found out yet just where notes stop.
During the Easter recess I walked around the Spadina riding from one end to the other. I could not find any wheat being grown there. There was a lot being consumed, but none being grown; so I can assure you, I am not going to speak about wheat at this time. Spadina riding is in a unique situation. We have a federal riding and within that federal riding are two provincial ridings. As
The Budget-Mr. Rea
many of you know, Spadina is one of the most cosmopolitan ridings in Canada. Let me show you why I say that. The representative of one of our provincial ridings is a Canadian of Ukrainian origin. The other provincial member is a Canadian of the Jewish faith, and I happen to represent the area federally. In my opinion this seems to indicate a tremendous growth in the thinking of people in Canada. It indicates a tremendous growth in democratic thinking, and it is that kind of thinking that is going to make Canada a much bigger and better place in which all of us may live.
I have never used the expression "new Canadian", because although I happen to be a third generation Canadian the man who received his citizenship papers this morning is just as good a Canadian as I am and is entitled to everything I am, so why should he be classified any differently? I wonder whether we all realize just what an immigrant goes through when he first comes to this country. In the province of Ontario alone there are 12 communist ethnic papers which are trying to sell their propaganda to the new immigrant, in his own language. Here is something that is hard to believe. These newspapers stress the fact that a Canadian communist is different from a Russian communist. I cannot emphasize too strongly how powerful a suggestion that is. As I said, there are 12 communist newspapers published in Ontario, and there are about twice that number in the whole of Canada. They have an estimated circulation of over
100.000	copies. They are published in 10 different languages. These newspapers are financed and managed from a central office in Toronto and, according to very reliable sources, one-quarter of a million dollars annually is the sum necessary to support the 12 in Ontario.
To offset that the democratic foreign language press in Ontario publishes about 35 newspapers and magazines in over 15 languages. There are 51 of these published in the whole of Canada in 22 languages, with a readership of about one million per week.
I wonder whether hon. members realize the silent warfare that is going on between those two bitterly opposed groups just for the minds of our immigrants. We all know that since the end of world war II approximately 1\ million immigrants have come to Canada, and it is estimated that close to
900.000	of those have come from non-English speaking parts of Europe. These immigrants have brought to Canada millions and millions of dollars in actual money. An estimate would place this in excess of about $500 million, since the end of world war II. We also find that these immigrants help to create jobs, because they buy a lot of goods and in many
2840	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Rea instances actually start their own businesses. A great many people believe-you have heard the remark, too-that these immigrants crowd many families into one house. This is completely wrong. According to a survey made about two years ago, of 128,000 immigrant households, 50,000 of the post-war immigrants own their own homes. A majority were single detached dwellings with all facilities. Of these, over 14,000 were entirely clear of mortgages. The remainder of the 128,000 averaged more than four rooms per household.
Bear in mind that for every worker we get almost one additional independent person, which helps to create additional consumer markets. Also remember that the minute those people go to work they become taxpayers and share the costs of running the country on all levels, be they municipal, provincial or federal. With that thought in mind I feel that since Canada has spent millions of dollars to get these people here- and it is an expenditure with which I agree, and I only wish we were getting a great many more immigrants-we should start to do more to educate those immigrants while they are going through the process of getting ready to become citizens.
Our investment in these people has started on the federal level, and it should carry on from the federal level. One of the ways to do this would be to support those democratic foreign language newspapers and magazines by advertising from every department of government. These advertisements could be in the form of educational information, describing the particular department. For example, the Department of National Health and Welfare could explain what it does; the Department of Labour could explain legislation affecting the workers; the Department of National Defence could explain its recruiting messages to those people who have been in this country long enough to be eligible for the armed forces.
I know the government does not think too much of this particular idea, because it does not want the outside world to think that it is recruiting men for the armed forces. But if these people are to become Canadians they should be entitled to all this information. The Post Office Department could tell them about its services, its rates, and particularly its overseas regulations. This could also work with the various other departments of government.
Remember, as I mentioned before, the bitter struggle that is being waged between the communists who are trying to win these people over to their ways, and the democratic foreign language papers that are trying to keep them our way. We must remember that these hew people naturally write letters back


home, and if those letters are full of praise and understanding about the ways in Canada, do you not think that will help to get more immigrants of the right kind out here?
I realize, of course, that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration does place advertising in these papers, but outside of the odd spasmodic advertisements by that department, one from the post office, and one from the R.C.M.P. about once a year, that is all the help these papers get that are doing more than anything else to explain democracy to these new people of ours.
A recent survey shows that in answer to the question put to these new immigrants, "Do you prefer reading your own language publications?" 96 per cent replied "Yes". To another question, "Do you receive one or more English weekly, bi-weekly or monthly magazines?", 80 [DOT] 1 per cent said they did not receive any of those. Therefore it is fairly obvious that the way to offset communist propaganda and to educate and tell these immigrants the wonderful opportunities that are here for them would be to support these democratic foreign language papers in a practical way through advertising.
I realize, of course, that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration does have a liaison group that tries to offset any communist effects, but it reaches such a small portion of these people that I am sure my suggestion would have a much greater effect. When these immigrants eventually become citizens -and remember, they have had to go through a lot to get to this point-many of us are fortunate enough to be able to adopt children. We all know the time comes when they are going to be asked the question, what does adoption mean? Perhaps most of these parents will wait until the child is old enough to understand. They will then take the children on their knees and say, "We looked at all the children in the world and out of all those children we chose you".
That is why I say that the immigrant who receives his citizenship papers has a big advantage over those of us who were born here, because when he gets his papers he can step outside and say, "Out of all the countries in the world, Canada, I chose you". In Spadina riding there are a great many people who have said and are waiting to say, "Canada, I chose you".
Since this speech is on the budget I am going to say something about it. During the Easter recess, besides walking around my riding I wanted to check and get some comments about this budget. We have heard a lot about television programs. The one I am going to refer to is on the list of those imported from the United States. When the

people in this particular program want some information they send out something which they call an A.P.B. I did not send out an A.P.B. to get the information I wanted; I sent out a W.I.T.B., which means "What is in the budget?" I sat back and waited, and it was not long before the answers started to come in. I received a flood of them, but the funniest thing I found in analysing them was that they were all the same. They were composed of just one word; "nothing".
I would like to make a few suggestions on a serious note to the Minister of Finance for his consideration. It might help some of those of us who are working people. For example, there are many jobs in which the man or woman employed has to wear a uniform. They pay for it themselves, and they are allowed no deductions when making out their income tax returns. This uniform helps them to earn their income, and it can be worn only when they are working. I can see no reason why it could not be classed as a deduction.
Let me give another example. In metropolitan Toronto we have more than one zone for street car fares. With new homes being built on the outskirts of the city we have this problem. The man or woman who lives on the outskirts and works toward the centre of the city, or the man or woman who lives in the centre and works toward the outskirts of the city, has to pay more than one fare. I cannot see why the government would not allow a person to deduct the extra fares that are paid as a legitimate expense. This would not be too difficult to handle, because the firm could verify the individual's correct address and could also verify the number of days he worked in the current year. I do not know whether hon. members realize just how much these extra fares can amount to in a year; they can run from $10 to $12 a month, or close to $120 a year.
Everyone has been trying to encourage people to buy their own homes; yet the interest they pay on their mortgages is not deductible in relation to private homes, and the cost of improvements to their homes is not deductible. The home is the basic foundation of this country, and if the government is going to encourage people to buy their own homes it should allow these people to deduct the interest on mortgages when paying their income tax.
We have had many statements in the house recently pointing to the deplorable shortage of engineers, scientists and teachers. This government has gone so far as to allow a foreign country to choose a foreign contractor for the D.E.W. project for the next three years because we are not capable of handling
The Budget-Mr. Rea the work. Here is something that Dean Woodside of the University of Toronto said:
If present trends continue there will be a desperate shortage of science teachers. The quality of students entering science courses will inevitably decline and the ultimate result for the schools, for the universities, and for all the many areas of society in which science is important might be disastrous.
We have also had several hon. members talk about the fact that scholarships should be made available in various forms, yet this same government which admits to these shortages does not do enough to encourage parents to send their children to university. After a boy or girl reaches a certain age the parents are allowed more deductions, but let us realize it is when a boy or girl enters university that the cost of education begins to reach its peak. Those of us who have struggled and are now struggling to put our own children through university are well acquainted with the costliness of university education. Why cannot the government be a leader in trying to overcome this admitted shortage by giving more tax relief, at the very least, for the parents?
I should like to refer briefly to the 20 per cent tax on Canadian editions of United States magazines. This subject has been adequately covered by one of the hon. members on this side of the house. I agree that the only reason anyone buys a magazine is that he thinks it is going to interest him, regardless of whether it is printed in the United States or Canada. I was always of the opinion that the job of the Department of Finance is to raise revenue as required, instead of doing what perhaps should be done by the customs department.
I would like to say a few words about the P P-P.-the poorly paid postman. I understand, of course, that certain raises are going through as reported in the press, but even those are not sufficient. Postal employees are victims of the government, which stresses job security as a bait to attract them. The maximum salary paid to a letter carrier in Canada is slightly less than the minimum starting salary paid to a letter carrier in the United States.
How pitifully inadequate are the salaries paid to postal employees. This is apparent from the fact that numerous postal employees desirous of building their own homes under the N.H.A., which is sponsored by this government, are refused loans because then-annual income is below the minimum required to insure that the applicant is a worth-while risk. In other words our government, which inaugurated the N.H.A. plan to provide the average working man with the opportunity of building and owning his own home, refuses to pay its own employees a decent annual

The Budget-Mr. Rea salary in order that they may qualify for a house under the government's own scheme. Certainly this situation is fantastic.
As one postman who has been in the service for some considerable time remarked, "I am the father of two grown girls, and it is rather humiliating that both my youngsters were able to get jobs and earn more money that I am earning after 25 years of service". The time has come for a general salary increase.
I should like to refer to another matter which was mentioned previously by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton). I think we have all been very shocked at the number of lives lost in this area due to fires since the first of the year. There is one cause of many of these fires which the government appears to choose to ignore for various reasons; that is the continued importing of substandard portable lamps and residential lighting fixtures. This government knows all about this matter, yet what is it doing about it? Absolutely nothing. I have mentioned the tragic loss of lives in this particular area since the first of the year without having referred to the loss of life throughout Canada. Let me quote something which appeared in the Financial Post of October 1, 1955:
Electrical fires have cost Canada $55 million since 1950.
Is that not an appalling situation? The Canadian industry manufacturing these articles is not asking for higher tariffs but simply feels that foreign manufacturers should be required to make their products to the same rigid standards set up by the government which apply to Canadian products. The Canadian lamp and fixture manufacturers must have their products approved and must sign a contract for this approved service before offering them for sale. Why can foreign manufacturers bring in cheap, unsafe merchandise to compete with Canadian merchandise? We have the Food and Drugs Act and other acts to safeguard Canadians. What are we doing about this situation? Absolutely nothing.
The government has said that it wants to be sure it has the support of the provinces before it intervenes in this field, yet how is it going to find this out if it does not try? The government already has had very favourable indications and comments from the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario; the department of labour of the province of Manitoba, under whose jurisdiction this comes; the department of labour of the province of Saskatchewan; the electric light and power department of Edmonton; the department of industries and labour of Edmonton; the electric energy inspection


department of Vancouver; the city electrician's office in the city of Moncton and others.
Why cannot this government take the lead and call the provinces together to discuss this matter and find a solution? Someone has to start the ball rolling, and I feel it is the responsibility of the federal government. Are we going to have to wait until more Canadians perish in fires as a result of these poor and unsafe electrical items? Let us stop trying to pass the buck between the provincial and federal governments. Let the federal government take the lead and summon the provinces together before more lives are lost.
Although I have been in Ottawa for a short time only, I could never understand why members of parliament were not allowed passes on T.C.A. A short time ago I discovered that the claim adjusters of the Canadian National Railways all have passes on T.C.A. I wondered about this, and the only comment I have to make at this time is this. I suppose when a train accident occurs the government wants to get the claim adjusters to the scene of the accident as quickly as possible to take statements from the people before they have a chance to discuss their claims with their lawyers. Of course that is what all adjusters do. I say it is just as important that hon. members who live some distance from Ottawa should be placed in a position where they can go home from time to time in order to find out what is going on in their ridings and, as an hon. member says, settle their claims as well.
I should like to say one or two things about the shipment of arms to Israel. I am and always have been in favour of the shipment of arms to Israel, because this would put the Jews in a position to defend themselves if they were attacked. I think you will agree that Egypt's actions in recent days have shown this to be a fact. I cannot understand why more definite action was not taken sooner by the United Nations which created the state of Israel, because everyone realized that trouble was bound to occur; but nothing seemed to be done until the fighting started to look serious. Then everyone started flying all over the world for conferences and talks to stop it. Perhaps this is just another one of those cases which have shown up so often of being too late, too late. I certainly hope not.
When listening to someone speak the other day I gathered this one little thought which I should like to pass on to the government for what it is worth:
Men are not free to do what they will-that is anarchy.

Men are not free to do what they must-that is compulsion.
Men are free to do what they ought-that is democracy.
That is what I urge the government to be, a democracy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer). It is unfortunate that the hon. member did not choose the right place to make it. In fact his speech would have been quite appropriate on the floor of the Quebec legislature where he would surely have convinced his provincial colleague of Three Rivers not to give away our natural resources to the Americans.
Moreover, if the hon. member will take a look at the Gazette of this morning, he will find the statements made last night by his friend, the premier of Quebec, on the opportunity of encouraging as much as possible the investment of American capital in Quebec. I quote:
Foreign capital is essential to our development.
That is what Messrs. Duplessis and Eaton stated.
Foreign capital-
Stated Mr. Duplessis.
-contrary to what some people seem to think-
And the hon. member for Three Rivers is among them, I suppose.
-is essential to the economic expansion of Quebec. Foreign capital, whether coming from France, from Great Britain or from the United States, is always welcome.
On the eve of an election in our province, I am grateful to the hon. member for Three Rivers who so generously endorses the demands of the provincial liberal leader as far as our natural resources are concerned although in doing so he is not very nice to his provincial friends to whom he owes so much.
As far as family allowances are concerned, I agree with the hon. member for Three Rivers when he says that a readjustment of the rates would be appropriate. However, the Canadian people are very happy to be able to take advantage of such a beneficial legislation enacted by a Liberal administration, and the hon. member for Three Rivers should be the last to criticize it knowing as he does that, with his leader, there would be no such thing.
Mr. Speaker, in the course of everyday life, -we often hear people talking of the variety of things from one day to the other and conclude most of the time by the old saying "Who knows what tomorrow may hold". The only 67509-180
The Budget-Mr. Roy ones who can flatter themselves for not being subjected to this rule are the members of this house. On the opposition side, from one session to the other, we always hear them repeating the same old thing. For some, the government has failed lamentably in its task; for others, the government is keeping the people of Canada in ignorance of the impending crash of the country's economy. Finally, for another section, the government has been living on hopes and Canadians find themselves in dire poverty and fear imminent disaster.
However, members on government benches are forced to repeat the same optimistic statements because of the fact that, every year, they find that we have made another step to a new high in all fields, political, commercial, economic and social. Therefore, everybody being free to analyse the economic data concerning this country, it is easy to ascertain the gradual changes that have come over our national economy. We will note, as a matter of fact, that from year to year and particularly since the last war, the revenue of the worker has improved, that profits are higher, the building trade more active and operations of all kinds more numerous than ever. But the statistical data on these subjects is more revealing still, on many scores.
In 1939 the gross national product was five billion 700 million dollars; in 1946 it had risen to 12 billion, and in 1953 to 23 billion. The expected figure for the current year is a record 28 billion.
This gradual improvement in the general economy has obvious repercussions in various areas of production and more particularly as regards wood products, mineral production, manufacturing, agriculture and labour, where the difference is even more marked.
Then there is a very special field where the contribution is even more tangible; it is that of the social reforms which have contributed to a large extent to maintain the Canadian way of life and the standard of living of the labouring class. In addition, these social measures have increased the economic security of most Canadians, and consequently that of trade and industry, through a more stable market. After 10 years, unemployment insurance benefits and social security contributions add up to several billion dollars and they are the factors which have contributed most to that stabilization and to economic prosperity in Canada.
For the last 10 years we have been confident, from year to year, in the future of

The Budget

Mr. Roy our country, and that confidence has been soundly justified because the Canadian people had put it in a Liberal government which did not fail in its duty. It is certainly not possible to obtain such vast transformation, such record expansion without a patch of shadow here and there. However, the expert handling of a sound and watchful administration has always been able to rectify the position without impeding the general progress towards a peak prosperity.
The prophets of doom, on the opposition side of the house, have had to revise their gloomy forecasts year after year.
Mr. Speaker, like every Canadian, I am pleased to note the improvement of the unemployment situation in this country, the willingness of the federal government to cooperate with the provinces in order to introduce some relief for the unemployed who are not insured. It seems there is a division of responsibilities and that this group of forgotten taxpayers will know a less anxious future.
We have been pleased to follow the discussions of the last federal-provincial meetings. They also seemed to warrant the hope of final achievement in various fields, like the tax agreements and the introduction of health insurance. I agree that, at first, the co-operation of my province in this respect has been cynical, but I am glad that some imminent atmospheric perturbations will soon permit a better understanding, which will lead to provincial co-operation, to a tax agreement and to the setting up of a national health insurance scheme to the best advantage of the people of my province.
Mr. Speaker, the farmers of my constituency asked me to congratuate the government on the way it has handled the problem of butter surplus and on its decision to maintain price support.
It is a pity however to see the different treatment inflicted on our Quebec farmers compared to those of the other provinces, just as a result of petty politics on the part of the government of my province. The farmers of my riding have just suffered two disastrous years, as a result of heavy rains two years ago, and of a drought last summer. Those two years have put the farmers into a very precarious situation. At the head of all those agricultural organizations, I pleaded with the federal Minister of Agriculture to help them in their plight, and he assured us of his willingness to help, provided naturally


that the province co-operates and recognizes its share of responsibility in that field. I will be greatly surprised if the generous contribution of the provincial administration consisted of anything but promises.
Mr. Speaker, I shall devote the greater part of the unexpired portion of my time to give my impressions of my trip to Mexico last May, when I was a member of the Canadian delegation to the eighth assembly of the world health organization.
WHO is an agency of the United Nations of which 57 countries are members. Its headquarters are located at Geneva, where the annual meetings of that organization are usually held.
This eighth assembly, held by exception away from the ordinary headquarters at Geneva, had for its main purpose to acquaint the delegates from oriental countries with the efforts made to solve the problems facing that part of the Americas lying within 25 degrees on either side of the equator. Mexico is one of the countries which are in great need of that help to solve their health problems.
General conferences of that organization, following the same pattern as a session of a democratic parliament, are held each year. The Canadian delegation to that eighth assembly was composed of four physicians: Dr. Moore, head of the Indian division in the Department of National Health and Welfare and president of the Canadian delegation; Dr. Curtis, head of the department of health of the province of Prince Edward Island; the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), myself and a few technicians of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I	am pleased to note at this point that I have the happiest recollections of the cordial relations which the members of the Canadian delegation enjoyed amongst themselves. I can assure the Minister of National Health and Welfare that this delegation did in no wise betray the trust which he had placed in it in choosing it to represent this country in a worthy fashion.
The Canadian delegation, along with those of the other member states, participated in the work of the committees set up by the plenary assembly of the world health organization. Members of the Canadian delegation sat on two of the main conference commissions: the agenda and budget commission and the administrative, financial and legal commission, presided over by Dr. Moore, of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the part played by Canada at these meetings is second in importance only to that of the great powers. Our country enjoys great prestige on the international scene. None more than the Canadian members of delegations sent to other countries are in a position to appreciate this fact. They have the great advantage of seeing how much consideration, confidence and sincere esteem our country, our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the leaders of our delegations to the United Nations, together with our democratic system and our sound administration, enjoy on the part of other countries of the world.
I wish at this point to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare for the kind attention he had for me in giving me this opportunity to join all those who just returned from this mission abroad, feeling greater pride of being a Canadian and loving one's country all the more.
The work of the WHO throughout the world is essential and it is to the credit of Canada that her government recognizes its responsibility and duty towards this work of international civilization. Of course, Canada is interested in this ultimate humanitarian aim of improving world health and is helping other members to that end. Thus, after only 8 years, the world is already benefiting from this co-operation thanks to the devotion of officers of WHO and to their achievements in the improvement of social medicine and the conquests of science over sources of infection and contagion, in the study of social and economic problems on which rests the improvement of health as well as in the contribution and wise distribution of public moneys. The coalition of science and charity in generous and devoted people cannot but bring about gigantic achievements against microbiological scourges which spread disease and death in most of the countries of the world.
Thus a tremendous amount of work has been done, and it has produced magnificent results. But, after hearing the delegations of the various countries make known their complaints, their needs and their wishes, one realizes that WHO is still far from the ultimate aim of its efforts. The health situation throughout the world is still very shaky and efforts of WHO will surely have to be much more fruitful, as far as financial contributions and the scope of activities are concerned, to enable it to do its work with a more concrete hope of bringing about radical and permanent achievements. No one could make better use than WHO of any generous contributions 67509-180J
The Budget-Mr. Roy from Canada and other members of the United Nations to ensure a minimum standard of health in the world.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that every effort on the part of the governments to achieve international peace will be ineffective, or fictitious as long as they do not establish the essential basis for this peace, that is the strength and energy to enjoy freedom, quietude and justice that only health can give. And this peace which our governments try to find at the price of such effort, will not be attained on the day when the United Nations have the supremacy of armaments and diplomacy, but when, in a universal gesture of charity and justice, they will have used all their efforts and energy for the conquest of the supreme physical and social welfare of all their member states.
How can we hope to achieve a universal political balance when more than half of mankind is still a victim of various plagues which science has overcome, but which are still, in actual fact, overpowering the vast majority of the world's peoples. How can a civilized and Christian world remain unaffected and indifferent in the knowledge that in the underdeveloped countries almost a billion people are suffering each year from swamp-fever, malaria and yellow fever?
Our world will not be able to claim it is civilized until the power of science and modern technology is made to serve human health everywhere.
In this twentieth century, after two dreadful world wars, men are striving to create a peaceful world. Indeed, there is nothing more essential nor more urgent in our time than to maintain world peace. Now, we all know that peace is not a simple political matter to be settled through agreements between nations, but that it hinges on the general progress of all nations. Peace is different from armed truce. Peace means liberty and plenty, justice and respect for man, a decent standard of living and above all good health. It is not enough to say that all nations and all men are entitled to be free, to be treated with justice and to have enough to live. To enjoy all that and to live a full life one must be healthy.
Mr. Speaker, would you allow me a few more minutes? I am nearly through.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
The end of 1955 marked the tenth anniversary of the United Nations Organization. This is the time to take our bearings or, if you wish, to sum up the ideas and the accomplishments of that organization.
It must certainly be recognized that in spite of what may have been said by some people, this institution has done a tremendous and beneficial job, and Canada won an honourable position through its generous contributions in many fields.
But, on the other hand, has Canada contributed its full share, and should it not do much more, especially as regards the financial part of the plan of assistance to the underdeveloped countries. I believe, along with Canadian newspapers, that the prestige and impact of our civilization urgently require that the western world brings a brilliant evidence of Christian charity and of solidarity to these underdeveloped people. Therefore, we can but support the recent decision of the government to increase substantially its contributions to the fund for assistance to these poor countries, although we consider that this increase is but a minimum.
Mr. Speaker, any right-minded citizen cannot refrain from admiring what countries are doing today, through United Nations agencies, to improve the sanitary and economic conditions of the underdeveloped countries. By giving food to hungry people, by improving their health, and by bringing technical assistance to the underdeveloped countries, we can do more to achieve peace than by spending billions of dollars on armaments. This is the genuine task pertaining to the nations such as ours which can produce what the world urgently needs.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that, in Canada, we have to face a problem of food surpluses. I humbly submit that the government might divert a few millions from war items to buy and send this food to the countries that are in need of it. This would be the best way to stop war, a vigorous stimulant in favour of peace and a powerful antidote against communistic ideology. We are a Christian country and our religious principles recommend that we extend our fraternity to all the world. If the Christian doctrine asks that we feed the hungry, clothe the naked and nurse the sick, if our Christian faith is real, we should encourage the government to pass the necessary legislation to prove that our creed is not restricted to principles but finds its expression in deeds.
